title: Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart

concept.text: Therapeutic remuscularization would repair an injured adult human heart by creating enough new, living heart muscle to restore a clinically meaningful amount of pumping capacity. The new cardiomyocytes—the cells that contract to generate force—would need to survive, contribute useful mechanical work, and coordinate their activity with the existing heart. Replacing lost myocardium is the regenerative goal described in the supplied review; successful human treatment is not established by that evidence.

Conceptual scope: the capability could be pursued by stimulating existing cardiomyocytes to produce additional muscle or by implanting replacement cells or engineered muscle. These routes belong to the same concept when they restore functioning myocardium within the patient's existing heart. An improvement caused only by temporary signaling from administered cells would not, by itself, demonstrate remuscularization.

significance.text: Myocardial infarction can leave irreversible fibrosis, loss of cardiomyocytes, and chronic cardiac dysfunction. A treatment that durably restored integrated, force-generating muscle and improved patient outcomes would make an important component of that injury therapeutically reparable. The revolutionary capability would be recovery of useful muscle in the damaged heart, extending beyond management of the consequences of muscle loss.

Conditional implications: successful repair could improve pumping capacity and reduce the burden of heart failure, potentially delaying or avoiding mechanical support or transplantation for some patients. Those consequences require clinical demonstration; producing additional cardiomyocytes does not automatically establish fewer hospitalizations, longer survival, or less need for replacement therapies. The supplied evidence does not quantify the eligible population or establish how its size would compare with populations served by replacement hearts.

Limits of the repair analogy: replacing muscle would not necessarily eliminate the cause of continuing injury. Extension from infarct-related muscle loss to dilated cardiomyopathy would depend on the underlying disease, the condition of the remaining myocardium, and control of ongoing damage. Transplantation also supplies working myocardium through whole-organ replacement, so it would be misleading to suggest that all existing treatments merely manage failure without providing muscle. Remuscularization specifically seeks to repair the existing heart.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a controllable way to generate and integrate enough new contractile myocardium to improve the injured adult human heart safely and durably. Adult mammals have largely lost the ability to replace myocardium through cardiomyocyte proliferation. The supplied review identifies manipulation of cardiomyocyte maturation and cell-cycle control as a foundation for regenerative strategies, while reporting progress in adult-animal models rather than an established human therapy.

Engineering synthesis: stimulating endogenous regeneration would require productive formation of additional cardiomyocytes, rather than treating a cell-cycle signal alone as evidence of new muscle. It would also require sufficient control over the location, extent, and duration of proliferation, followed by muscle capable of performing useful work. An implantation approach would instead need a reproducible supply of suitable muscle, effective delivery, sustained survival, and adequate blood supply within the injured heart. These are requirements inferred from the proposed capability, not findings verified from the full review.

Engineering synthesis: either route must overcome integration at several levels. New tissue must receive adequate perfusion, transmit force through the ventricular wall, and contract in coordination with native myocardium without creating clinically important rhythm disturbances. Demonstrating additional muscle is therefore a separate task from demonstrating useful pumping work, and both are separate from establishing durable patient benefit. Imaging and histology can contribute evidence of tissue formation but cannot alone establish electrical coupling.

current_state.text: In “Molecular gatekeepers of endogenous adult mammalian cardiomyocyte proliferation,” published on 7 April 2025, Tim Koopmans and Eva van Rooij describe post-infarction fibrosis, cardiomyocyte death, and chronic dysfunction as a substantial clinical challenge without an available curative treatment. They also describe the largely lost proliferative capacity of adult mammalian cardiomyocytes. These are statements from a dated review, rather than a complete assessment of every clinical approach through November 2026.

The same review reports successful reactivation of cardiomyocyte cell-cycle induction in preclinical adult-animal models, accompanied by functional recovery after cardiac injury. This provides a biological basis for pursuing regeneration, but does not establish effective human remuscularization. The retained material includes the abstract and key points, with author information, rather than the full review. It does not provide sufficient inspected study detail here to assess individual models, effect sizes, durability, or translation to patients; figure captions and reference titles cannot substitute for those results.

The supplied research attributes several quantitative findings to the 2025 Circulation paper “A Latent Cardiomyocyte Regeneration Potential in Human Heart Disease”: carbon-14-based estimates of approximately 0.5% annual cardiomyocyte renewal in healthy adults, generation rates 18 to 50 times lower in end-stage heart failure, and increased renewal in some hearts unloaded with a ventricular assist device. The source index contains no retained text or artifact for that paper, so these figures and the unloading finding remain reported but unverified within this record. That evidence gap does not show that the findings are false. If confirmed, the unloading observation would be a clue to regenerative potential, rather than proof of a controllable remuscularization treatment.

The supplied material does not establish whether tested human cell products have produced remuscularization, nor does it substantiate the original blanket summary that two decades of cell therapy have failed to do so. It also contains no completed freshness search establishing clinical status as of 1 November 2026. The defensible conclusion is that the retained evidence documents a regenerative goal and preclinical progress, while leaving the human treatment record and subsequent developments unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in a defined population after substantial myocardial infarction or with an appropriately specified form of systolic heart failure, treatment should produce durable new myocardium and show that it contributes useful contractile work. Imaging and histology, where feasible and ethically obtainable, should establish tissue formation; complementary functional measurements should establish coordinated electrical activation and mechanical contribution. A transient paracrine improvement without new muscle would not satisfy this concept. These are proposed criteria, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Durable new myocardium contributes coordinated, useful contractile work

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical evidence: a randomized comparison against appropriate guideline-directed care should demonstrate a prespecified, clinically important improvement in ventricular function and a reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalization. Ejection fraction could be one functional endpoint, but no universal numerical cutoff is adopted here. The protocol should distinguish durable recovery from short-lived changes and define the clinically meaningful effect before outcomes are known.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized evidence shows ventricular improvement and reduced death or heart-failure hospitalization

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and safety boundaries: convincing completion would require independently reproducible benefit, sustained follow-up, and acceptable risks of arrhythmia, inappropriate tissue growth, immune complications where relevant, and delivery-related harm. The treatment should have reproducible manufacturing or delivery and a usable range of doses or treatment conditions. Follow-up duration and acceptable risk thresholds would need prospective justification rather than being assumed.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproducible benefit with prospectively justified safety and follow-up boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope of the conclusion: trials should specify injury type, disease cause, scar burden, baseline function, and concomitant treatment. Success in one population would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions; it would not prove effectiveness across every cardiomyopathy or literal universality. Failure to stop an ongoing disease process should also be distinguished from failure of the new muscle itself to survive or function.
completion_criteria.label: Conclusions limit demonstrated efficacy to specified trial populations

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: CLM-05, “Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale,” and CLM-11, “Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body,” overlap with this concept as possible routes to restoring cardiac function through replacement. CLM-06 centers on rebuilding muscle within an existing heart; the other entries concern donor-organ replacement or organs assembled outside the body. Engineered cardiac tissue could create a technical connection with CLM-11, but the supplied roster does not define whether that entry includes partial tissue constructs. No comparative claim about patient population size is established.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-04, “Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury,” and CLM-15, “Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney,” share the broader ambition of rebuilding functional biological structures after adult tissue loss. Their completion requirements remain distinct: coordinated cardiac contraction does not establish restored neural circuitry or new functioning nephrons. CLM-04 is broader than the earlier shorthand of reconnecting a severed spinal cord.

Roster-based comparison: CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” could overlap if genome writing were used to control cardiac regeneration, but remuscularization does not require that particular method, and genome writing alone would not demonstrate muscle restoration. CLM-01, “Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance,” could be relevant to implanted cells requiring immune acceptance, while CLM-08, “Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging,” could intersect with efforts to alter adult cell state. These are conditional connections inferred from the roster titles, not demonstrated dependencies or grounds for merging the entries.

unresolved_issues: The Circulation paper's identity and findings cannot be verified from retained document content; the renewal estimates, end-stage-failure comparison, and ventricular-unloading results remain unresolved.
The supplied record does not establish the complete history of human cell-product remuscularization or clinical developments through 1 November 2026.
The full Nature Reviews Cardiology review was not available in the retained preview, limiting assessment of individual preclinical studies, effect sizes, methods, durability, and safety.
Eligible patient numbers, comparative reach versus replacement-heart approaches, and effectiveness across different causes of dilated cardiomyopathy are not established.
A future demonstration protocol must specify measurements of electrical and mechanical contribution, follow-up duration, clinically meaningful effects, and acceptable safety boundaries.
The relationship between partial engineered cardiac tissue and CLM-11 remains undefined by the supplied roster title.

brief.title: New working muscle for a damaged heart
possible: After a heart attack, people could regain pumping strength through new living muscle in their own heart. Treatment could help surviving muscle cells multiply or implant replacement muscle that survives and beats with the heart.
why: A heart attack can leave permanent scar tissue and destroy muscle that supplies pumping force. Restoring that muscle could repair a lasting part of the damage and reduce the burden of heart failure.
For some patients, restoring enough pumping capacity could delay or avoid a mechanical pump or heart transplant.

sources.who: Tim Koopmans and Eva van Rooij
sources.showed: Their review reports that researchers have restarted the process of cell division in adult animal heart muscle cells, with recovery of heart function after injury.
sources.quote: leading to the successful reactivation of cell cycle induction in adult animals, with functional recovery after cardiac injury.
sources.cited_for: Adult animal results provide a biological basis for trying to replace lost heart muscle.
sources.not_established: Animal recovery does not establish that treatment can create lasting, coordinated muscle and improve outcomes in people.

sources.showed: This is a study of heart muscle cell renewal in human heart disease, including hearts supported by a mechanical pump.
sources.cited_for: It examines whether diseased human hearts retain the capacity to produce new muscle cells.
sources.not_established: Observing cell renewal does not establish a controllable treatment that restores useful pumping strength.

shown: Tim Koopmans and Eva van Rooij review adult animal experiments that restarted the process of heart muscle cell division and reported recovery after injury. These results support pursuing regeneration, but do not establish successful repair of an adult human heart.
missing: A treatment must create enough lasting new muscle in an injured adult human heart to restore useful pumping strength.
New muscle must receive blood, transmit force and beat with the existing heart without causing dangerous rhythms.
Controlled trials must show lasting improvements in heart function and patient outcomes.
Independent teams must reproduce the benefit with reliable treatment delivery and acceptable risks.

milestones.label: Lasting new muscle adds coordinated pumping force
milestones.explanation: New muscle would have to survive and contribute force while following the heart's electrical signals. This would establish actual muscle repair beyond a temporary benefit from signals released by treated cells.

milestones.label: Randomized trials show better pumping and fewer serious outcomes
milestones.explanation: A randomized trial against recommended care would have to show lasting, clinically meaningful pumping improvement and reduced death or hospital admission for heart failure. This would connect muscle repair to patient benefit.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce lasting benefit with acceptable risks
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce lasting benefit with reliable treatment production or delivery, usable doses and justified safety and follow-up limits. This would establish that repair can be repeated safely.

milestones.label: Results establish which patients benefit
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to define the injury, disease cause, scarring, starting function and other treatment of participants. This would limit claims to tested patients and distinguish ongoing disease from failure of new muscle.

uncertain: How much new muscle is enough to produce a clinically meaningful recovery?
Which measurements best establish that new muscle follows the heart's electrical signals and contributes pumping force?
How long must benefits last, which risks are acceptable, and which causes of heart failure could respond?

page.title: Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart
page.definition: Treatment restores myocardium, the heart's muscle tissue, by generating cardiomyocytes in an injured adult heart or transplanting them into its wall or onto its surface. The new muscle cells survive and contribute to the force of the heartbeat. That contribution improves heart-failure symptoms, physical function or survival.

goal.need: In 2021, an estimated 300,000 or more people in the United States had advanced heart failure. Medicines and devices can ease symptoms, and donor hearts are scarce. After a heart attack, scar can take the place of muscle that once pumped blood. Progressive cardiomyopathy can also deplete that muscle. For people limited by this loss, restoring pumping force could ease symptoms or make physical activity easier. The new cells must survive and contract, with a benefit large enough to justify risks such as abnormal heart rhythms.

completion.title: A controlled human study links new contractile myocardium to a clinical heart-failure benefit.
completion.criterion: A prespecified, adequate and well-controlled study in adults with heart failure demonstrates that newly generated or transplanted cardiomyocytes survive, contribute contractile work within the recipient heart, and mediate improvement in symptoms, physical function or survival. The protocol specifies the effect size, follow-up and safety acceptance criteria before enrolment.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis. No outside body identified defines the combined test of contractile contribution and controlled clinical benefit.
completion.basis: The cardiomyocyte consensus defines cell replacement, EMA asks for evidence of the mode of action, and FDA's draft guidance identifies symptoms, function and survival as clinical benefits. BioVAT-HF reported changes from baseline and documented surviving donor muscle in an explanted heart. HEAL-CHF found a greater improvement in six-minute walk distance with injected cells plus bypass surgery than with bypass alone. Neither study established how much of the patient benefit came from contraction by new muscle.

milestones.title: Treatment replaces lost cardiomyocytes in an injured adult mammalian heart.
milestones.criterion: Identify new cardiomyocytes in the treated heart and establish their origin. For proliferation of existing cardiomyocytes, demonstrate completed cell division into daughter cells. DNA synthesis and an increase in nuclei per cell can both occur without formation of a new cardiomyocyte. For transplantation, identify surviving graft-derived cardiomyocytes at the treated site.
milestones.set_by: International author consensus in Cardiomyocyte Regeneration: A Consensus Statement, definition of renewal and genetic fate-mapping convention.
milestones.threshold_quote: replace lost cardiomyocytes by new ones.

milestones.title: A stem-cell-based muscle product shows proof of principle and safety in a relevant animal model.
milestones.criterion: Before human administration, establish proof of principle and assess safety in an animal model relevant to the intended use. Justify the model and select follow-up appropriate to the cells' persistence and function. If a suitable model is unavailable and nonclinical evidence is insufficient, EMA calls for additional clinical efficacy or safety endpoints to address the gap.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Reflection paper on stem cell-based medicinal products, section 4. Written for stem-cell products.
milestones.threshold_quote: Nonclinical evidence on the proof-of-principle and safety of the stem-cell based product in a relevant animal model is expected before administration to humans.

milestones.title: At least two adults per BioVAT dose level complete an uneventful 28-day follow-up.
milestones.criterion: In BioVAT-HF Part A, assess at least two adults at each tested dose level for 28 days after implantation under immunosuppression. The planned levels are 5, 10 and 20 engineered-heart-muscle units. Dose escalation requires uneventful follow-up, with particular attention to procedure-related arrhythmias and worsening heart failure.
milestones.set_by: University Medical Center Göttingen, registered BioVAT-HF protocol NCT04396899, Part A, described in its peer-reviewed report. Written for engineered-muscle grafts.

milestones.title: Wall thickness, ejection fraction and health status increase from baseline at 3 months in BioVAT-HF.
milestones.criterion: At the safe maximal dose, test the change from baseline to 3 months in target-wall thickness, left ventricular ejection fraction and the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary Score. Ejection fraction is the share of ventricular blood volume ejected per beat. The questionnaire measures patient-reported health status. Assess increases in the three endpoints with the prespecified Hochberg procedure controlling the two-sided familywise error rate at 0.10.
milestones.set_by: University Medical Center Göttingen, BioVAT-HF prespecified interim analysis and statistical analysis plan, reported in the 28 May 2026 issue of the New England Journal of Medicine. Written for engineered-muscle grafts.
milestones.threshold_quote: two-sided level of 0.10 according to the Hochberg procedure.

milestones.title: A controlled human study establishes clinical benefit from a treatment intended to remuscularize the heart.
milestones.criterion: In adults with heart failure, demonstrate a prespecified improvement in symptoms, physical function or survival in an adequate and well-controlled study. Use a valid comparison group, measures to minimise bias and a quantitative comparison of the clinical outcome between groups.
milestones.set_by: US FDA, 21 CFR 314.126 and Treatment for Heart Failure: Endpoints for Drug Development, June 2019 draft guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: improves how a patient feels, functions (i.e., symptomatic or functional improvement), or survives.

milestones.title: Selectively suppressing graft contraction reduces ventricular function in an injured animal heart.
milestones.criterion: Measure ventricular function in a graft-bearing heart before, during and after selective, reversible inhibition of contraction by donor cardiomyocytes. Show a decrease in ventricular performance during inhibition that reverses when inhibition ends, and control for the effect of the stimulus on the recipient heart.
milestones.set_by: Experimental convention for testing active force contribution, applied by Stüdemann and colleagues and distinguished from comparisons of contractile and noncontractile grafts by Karbassi and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: switching off contractility in engrafted cardiomyocytes would result in a decrease in left ventricular function.

milestones.title: Donor cardiomyocytes are identified in a recipient's heart after implantation.
milestones.criterion: Identify cardiomyocytes at the implant site in recipient heart tissue obtained after implantation. Establish cardiomyocyte identity by tissue examination and confirm donor origin with a marker that distinguishes donor from recipient. Report the interval from implantation to tissue sampling.
milestones.set_by: Histological and donor-marker convention for graft identification, applied to human heart tissue by the BioVAT-HF investigators.
milestones.threshold_quote: clinical proof of CM retention after EHM implantation

not_found: No controlled human study jointly demonstrating new myocardium's contractile contribution and clinical benefit was located.
No position rejecting therapeutic remuscularization as a goal was identified in the cardiology society, programme or regulatory documents examined.

definition = "Treatment restores myocardium, the heart's muscle tissue, by generating cardiomyocytes in an injured adult heart or transplanting them into its wall or onto its surface. The new muscle cells survive and contribute to the force of the heartbeat. That contribution improves heart-failure symptoms, physical function or survival.". Reason: The phrase “within an injured adult heart” can exclude a graft on the heart's outer surface, where donor muscle has already been identified in a patient.

goal.need = "In 2021, an estimated 300,000 or more people in the United States had advanced heart failure. Medicines and devices can ease symptoms, and donor hearts are scarce. After a heart attack, scar can take the place of muscle that once pumped blood. Progressive cardiomyopathy can also deplete that muscle. For people limited by this loss, restoring pumping force could ease symptoms or make physical activity easier. The new cells must survive and contract, with a benefit large enough to justify risks such as abnormal heart rhythms.". Reason: The current text gives a study sample in place of the patient burden and omits the higher renewal rate in patients who responded to ventricular assist support.

add statement by European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart, 2019: "Cardiac cell-based TE aims to remuscularize post-infarct myocardial scars". Reason: The 2019 position paper records a professional society working group's explicit goal of remuscularizing infarct scars.

edit completion: set_by = "Atlas synthesis. No outside body identified defines the combined test of contractile contribution and controlled clinical benefit."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; basis = "The cardiomyocyte consensus defines cell replacement, EMA asks for evidence of the mode of action, and FDA's draft guidance identifies symptoms, function and survival as clinical benefits. BioVAT-HF reported changes from baseline and documented surviving donor muscle in an explanted heart. HEAL-CHF found a greater improvement in six-minute walk distance with injected cells plus bypass surgery than with bypass alone. Neither study established how much of the patient benefit came from contraction by new muscle."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14]. Reason: The basis omits the randomized HEAL-CHF result, which bears directly on the distinction between a treatment effect and the force supplied by new muscle.
add case "Endogenous muscle regeneration". Reason: Generating new muscle from cells already in the recipient requires evidence of new cell formation in that heart.
add case "Cell injection". Reason: HEAL-CHF tested cells injected into the ventricular wall, a route with its own evidence on function and arrhythmias.
add case "Engineered tissue implantation". Reason: BioVAT-HF tested preformed muscle on the heart's surface, and its dose-escalation and interim efficacy rules apply to that graft.

edit m1: title = "Treatment replaces lost cardiomyocytes in an injured adult mammalian heart."; criterion = "Identify new cardiomyocytes in the treated heart and establish their origin. For proliferation of existing cardiomyocytes, demonstrate completed cell division into daughter cells. DNA synthesis and an increase in nuclei per cell can both occur without formation of a new cardiomyocyte. For transplantation, identify surviving graft-derived cardiomyocytes at the treated site."; threshold_quote = "replace lost cardiomyocytes by new ones."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 8, 9, 10, 19]. Reason: The criterion mixes study results with the test and leaves unclear how to distinguish new cells from DNA replication in an existing cell.

add milestone after m1: "Selectively suppressing graft contraction reduces ventricular function in an injured animal heart.". Reason: A selective test of graft contraction fills the gap between finding new cells and showing that they help the ventricle pump.

edit m2: title = "A stem-cell-based muscle product shows proof of principle and safety in a relevant animal model."; criterion = "Before human administration, establish proof of principle and assess safety in an animal model relevant to the intended use. If a suitable model is unavailable and nonclinical evidence is insufficient, EMA calls for additional clinical efficacy or safety endpoints to address the gap."; threshold_quote = "Nonclinical evidence on the proof-of-principle and safety of the stem-cell based product in a relevant animal model is expected before administration to humans."; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 10]. Reason: The current criterion embeds macaque outcomes and the title extends EMA's stem-cell product guidance to every remuscularization approach.

edit m3: title = "At least two adults per BioVAT dose level complete an uneventful 28-day follow-up."; criterion = "In BioVAT-HF Part A, assess at least two adults at each tested dose level for 28 days after implantation under immunosuppression. The planned levels are 5, 10 and 20 engineered-heart-muscle units. Dose escalation requires uneventful follow-up, with particular attention to procedure-related arrhythmias and worsening heart failure."; threshold_quote = "uneventful follow-up for 28 days"; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7, 20]. Reason: Adverse-event counts and a finding from an explanted heart obscure the protocol's specific 28-day dose-escalation rule.

add milestone after m3: "Donor cardiomyocytes are identified in a recipient's heart after implantation.". Reason: Human graft survival is a distinct anatomical finding that the existing entry places inside a dose-tolerance criterion.

edit m4: title = "Wall thickness, ejection fraction and health status increase from baseline at 3 months in BioVAT-HF."; criterion = "At the safe maximal dose, test the change from baseline to 3 months in target-wall thickness, left ventricular ejection fraction and the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary Score. Assess increases in the three endpoints with the prespecified Hochberg procedure controlling the two-sided familywise error rate at 0.10."; threshold_quote = "two-sided level of 0.10 according to the Hochberg procedure."; threshold_ref = 7; refs = [7].
